title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) that tested whether deterministic verifier augmentation (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals from a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 unique intent→configuration tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) a guarded pipeline (gpt-5-mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one LLM call per task) yielding model_calls_used = 200. Results (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0). Paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that the deterministic verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this execution. We publish the complete preregistered run and artifacts, present an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of this testability failure, and give concrete, archive‑supported design recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration using the reserved exploratory budget, and deterministic pilot checks) to enable informative repeats.

sections.introduction:
Automated translation from operator intent to device configuration using large language models (LLMs) promises to reduce human workload in network operations (NetOps). However, incorrect or improperly ordered changes can cause outages, broken reachability, or policy violations. Tool‑augmentation—pairing LLM generation with deterministic validators, sandboxed simulators, or constrained executors in generate–validate–repair pipelines—has been proposed to mitigate these risks. We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment to measure whether a deterministic verifier reduces verifier‑detected unsafe proposals produced by a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial prompt transforms.

Research question. How does deterministic tool‑augmentation (generate → deterministic verifier → optional repair) change the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe network‑change proposals produced by a hosted LLM under preregistered adversarial and benign prompt clusters? The primary estimand was the paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) evaluated by an exact McNemar two‑sided test with a paired bootstrap CI.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, archived, deterministic paired run (N=200 tasks) comparing baseline LLM generation to a verifier‑augmented pipeline; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis explaining why the execution produced a degenerate ceiling outcome that rendered the preregistered confirmatory test non‑informative; (3) concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations for informative repeats and alternative estimands that preserve inferential validity under resource constraints. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived in the study bundle (manifested in the preregistration and execution records).
sections.related_work:
Surveys and prototype reports document rapid interest in LLMs for NetOps tasks (intent translation, configuration synthesis, and limited remediation) and repeatedly emphasize both promise and safety concerns [1,2,3]. A common architectural response is tool‑augmentation: combining LLM generation with deterministic validators, sandbox replay, or constrained executors in generate–validate–refine or divide–verify–refine pipelines. Experimental and methodological reports show these pipelines can reduce explicit constraint violations on curated tasks when the external verifier faithfully encodes domain constraints, but effect sizes depend strongly on verifier fidelity and evaluation semantics (sampling, repair policies, and generation budgeting) [4,5,6].

Prior work on guardrails, schema‑based tool interfaces, and agent orchestration emphasizes practical trade‑offs: stricter verifier schemas may lower unsafe acceptances but can increase false refusals and operator burden if the verifier is incomplete or overly conservative [3,7]. Red‑teaming studies in related domains recommend ROC‑style diagnostics for verifier behaviour and advance the need for replayable, workflow‑centred evaluation (explicit initial/final states, deterministic task generators, and archived validator traces). Our study aligns with these prescriptions by preregistering a paired estimand, using a deterministic task generator, sandboxed deterministic validation, and archiving full validator traces to permit deterministic replay and independent audit [1,4,5].
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study was preregistered as cand-2026-01-prereg-v1. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (guarded − baseline) on binary SAFE indicators returned by a deterministic sandbox validator. Confirmatory test: exact two‑sided McNemar; CIs: paired bootstrap percentile (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). The preregistration specified a paired binary design with N=200 tasks, planned paired episodes = 400, and a power analysis targeting detection of ≈7 percentage‑point reductions given an assumed baseline unsafe rate ≈10–15%.

Task generation and scope. A deterministic task generator produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks constrained to a single‑AS multi‑device family and limited to three fields (admin, mtu, vlan). Each task manifest included initial_state, expected_final_state, explicit workflow policies (required_sequence), and difficulty metadata. Tasks were clustered into benign and adversarial prompt transforms using a preregistered obfuscation template set; the adversarial cluster was included among confirmatory items per the preregistration.

Compared pipelines and generation semantics. Baseline: LLM candidate accepted and scored post hoc by the deterministic validator. Guarded: the same LLM candidate validated in a deterministic sandbox using deterministic_netops_validator_v5; in the confirmatory episodes repair paths were not invoked (repair traces are null) so the guarded arm performed validation only. The preregistration allowed two generation semantics: independent per‑arm generation (two model calls per task) or shared_initial_candidate (one LLM call per task scored by both arms). To conserve model budget the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), which produces one shared candidate per task that both arms score.

Modeling, validation, and analysis pipeline. Declared model: gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json). Validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementing full_intent_constraint_validation and emitting deterministic valid/violation outputs. Confirmatory outcomes derive from validator.valid (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE). Analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 computed contingency counts (n11,n10,n01,n00), exact McNemar two‑sided p‑value, and paired bootstrap CI (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). Missingness and retry rules (one automatic retry per failed model call; deterministic exclusion/replacement rules) were applied as preregistered. All design choices and seeds are archived in the preregistration and execution manifests; the archive contains full scoring JSONs and validator traces permitting deterministic replay.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The execution manifest reports completed_episode_count = 400 (200 paired episodes), failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 200, consistent with the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and the preregistered model budgeting choice. Provider audit confirmed hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and no cross‑condition cache reuse; deterministic reconciliation checks passed, indicating no technical failures or nondeterministic verifier behaviour in the confirmatory set.

Primary confirmatory outcomes. The deterministic validator labeled every confirmatory episode as SAFE: baseline SAFE = 200/200 and guarded SAFE = 200/200. Paired contingency counts: n11 = 200 (SAFE in both), n10 = 0 (SAFE only guarded), n01 = 0 (SAFE only baseline), n00 = 0 (UNSAFE in both). From these counts the paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Representative scoring JSONs in the archive show identical shared_initial_candidate text across arms and validator traces with violation_count = 0 and repair_provider_trace = null for confirmatory episodes; these traces explain the degenerate contingency.

Interpretation. The degenerate contingency (no discordant pairs) makes the preregistered paired inferential test non‑informative for the intended causal estimand. McNemar's test requires discordant pairs (n10 and n01) to estimate a paired difference; under shared generation semantics and with zero baseline unsafe rate there was no arm‑level variation to attribute to the verifier. The executed semantics therefore prevented the study from exercising the mechanism by which a verifier could demonstrably reduce unsafe proposals (either by rejecting an unsafe candidate or by applying repairs that change the guarded arm's outcome).
sections.discussion:
Root cause diagnosis (artifact‑grounded). Three archived facts jointly produced the non‑informative outcome: (1) generation semantics: the run used shared_initial_candidate so each paired episode had only one LLM candidate that both arms evaluated; (2) validator outcomes: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 rated all sampled candidates as valid (baseline SAFE = 200/200); and (3) repairs: repair_provider_trace fields are null in confirmatory scoring JSONs, so the guarded arm did not alter candidates. Because no arm‑specific stochasticity or repair‑driven changes occurred, the arms could not disagree and the paired contrast could not be realized. These facts are present in the execution and scoring artifacts archived with the run.

Design implications and recommendations (archive‑supported). To obtain an informative paired causal contrast the estimand must be matched to generation semantics and resource budgeting. Concrete recommendations, each traceable to preregistered budget accounting and scoring traces, are: (A) use independent per‑arm generation for confirmatory paired contrasts unless the guarded arm deterministically repairs candidates in a reproducible way; independent generation for N=200 requires ≈200 additional model calls (400 total) compared with shared semantics, visible in the preregistered execution_contract and execution manifest; (B) consume a preregistered exploratory reserve (we reserved up to 50 tasks) to calibrate adversarial transforms until the baseline unsafe rate aligns with the power assumptions; archive these calibration runs and fix transform parameters before confirmatory execution; (C) include a deterministic pilot check on a small holdout prior to the full confirmatory set and abort the confirmatory test if the pilot shows a ceiling/floor contingency—then follow preregistered contingency‑preserving adaptation paths (e.g., enable independent draws or strengthen adversarial injections); and (D) if repairs are allowed in the guarded arm, instrument and analyze repair_provider_trace artifacts to quantify UNSAFE→SAFE conversions and to verify that repairs do not introduce new violations.

Alternative estimands under tight budgets. When independent per‑arm generation is infeasible, adopt estimands compatible with shared semantics: estimate the absolute unsafe‑proposal rate of the LLM baseline with CIs; estimate guardrail refusal and post‑repair SAFE rates (requires enabling repairs and archiving repair traces); or use exploratory ROC estimation to characterize validator true/false positive behaviour (consumes the exploratory reserve). The preregistration enumerated these secondary and exploratory estimands; selecting them a priori preserves inferential validity.

Threats to validity and external generalization. Internal validity: the shared_generation choice constrained arm‑level variation and is the proximate cause of the non‑informative outcome. Construct validity: our validator encodes full_intent_constraint_validation for the synthetic task family (admin/mtu/vlan fields); its completeness relative to production failure modes is limited. External validity: tasks are synthetic single‑AS topologies; results do not generalize to multi‑AS, multi‑vendor, or richer configuration spaces. Conclusion validity: the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline unsafe rate; that assumption failed here, invalidating the original power analysis. These limitations are archived and reported in the study bundle.

Operational implications. Operator teams must weigh the incremental model‑call cost of independent per‑arm draws or exploratory calibration against the operational risk of unverified changes. Our artifacts make the per‑task resource arithmetic explicit (executed model_calls_used = 200 vs preregistered maximum for independent draws = 400) so operators can quantify this trade‑off before committing to confirmatory designs or production experiments.

Reproducibility. All artifacts necessary to replay the run deterministically—task manifests, shared responses, scoring JSONs, execution manifest, model configuration, and analysis artifacts—are archived in the study bundle. The archive contains the exact bootstrap parameters and the analysis contingency table that reproduce the numerical outputs reported above. Readers and future experimenters should consult these artifacts before altering preregistered design choices.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived, preregistered paired experiment comparing gpt-5-mini baseline generation and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0,0.0]). Because identical per‑pair generations were used and because the baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis was not testable in this run. The study's substantive contribution is methodological and reproducibility‑centred: (1) a complete deterministic preregistered run with archived artifacts permitting exact replay; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis explaining why the execution was non‑informative for verifier efficacy; and (3) concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration using reserved exploratory items, pilot contingency checks, and repair instrumentation) for informative repeats. The archived artifacts permit deterministic replication of the outcome and should be consulted prior to attempts to repeat or extend this experiment.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups; results may not generalize to production multi‑AS, multi‑vendor, or richer configuration features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt-5-mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or explicit injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
